group.title: Formal linking words
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: In addition to what has been said.
examples: The flat is cheap. {Furthermore}, it is near the station.
wrong: The flat is cheap. Furthermore, it is very expensive.

examples: The plan is costly; {moreover}, it will take years.
wrong: The food was cold. Moreover, it was hot.

words.meaning: Despite what has just been said.
examples: It was raining. {Nevertheless}, we went for a walk.
wrong: It was sunny. Nevertheless, it was a sunny day.

words.meaning: Used to compare two different facts.
examples: I like tea, {whereas} my sister prefers coffee.
wrong: I like tea, whereas I also like tea.

examples: We played {despite} the rain.
wrong: We played despite the perfect sunny weather.

examples: He finished the race {in spite of} his injury.
wrong: She won in spite of her excellent training.

examples: He missed the bus; {consequently}, he was late.
wrong: He left early; consequently, he was late.

words.meaning: In this way; for this reason.
examples: Sales fell; {thus} the shop had to close.
wrong: Sales rose; thus the shop had to close because of low sales.

examples: I cooked dinner. {Meanwhile}, she set the table.
wrong: First I cooked, and meanwhile, a week later, she set the table.

words.meaning: In a way that is almost the same.
examples: Cats need care; {similarly}, dogs need attention.
wrong: Cats like fish; similarly, dogs hate fish completely.

examples: He was polite, and I did {likewise}.
wrong: She smiled, and I did likewise by frowning.

examples: {In addition}, the hotel has a pool.
wrong: The hotel is great. In addition, it is terrible.

words.meaning: Used to give a different point of view.
examples: The job pays well. {On the other hand}, the hours are long.
wrong: The job pays well. On the other hand, the money is great.

words.meaning: Used to show a clear difference.
examples: The north is wet. {In contrast}, the south is dry.
wrong: The north is wet. In contrast, the south is wet too.

examples: It snowed. {As a result}, schools closed.
wrong: It was sunny. As a result, schools closed because of the snow.

examples: The flight was late {due to} fog.
wrong: The flight was on time due to the fog that delayed it.

examples: The match was cancelled {owing to} rain.
wrong: The match went ahead owing to the rain that cancelled it.

examples: You can go {provided that} you finish your work.
wrong: You can go provided that you never finish your work, which you must finish.

examples: It may rain, but we’ll go {regardless}.
wrong: It might rain, so we’ll go regardless only if it is sunny.

words.meaning: Used to give exact details of what you just mentioned.
examples: Two students, {namely} Ana and Ben, won prizes.
wrong: Two students won, namely nobody.

examples: {Overall}, the trip was a success.
wrong: Overall, looking only at one small detail, it was good.

examples: I like Italian food, pasta {in particular}.
wrong: I like all Italian food, in particular nothing.

examples: I agree with you {to some extent}.
wrong: I agree to some extent; I agree with every single word.

words.meaning: Used to accept that something is true.
examples: {Admittedly}, the plan has some risks.
wrong: Admittedly, the plan has risks, which I strongly deny.

words.meaning: Used to say what you think is probably true.
examples: {Presumably}, the train is delayed.
wrong: Presumably the train is late; I know this for a fact because I am driving it.

words.meaning: According to what you have heard.
examples: {Apparently}, the shop is closing.
wrong: Apparently the shop is closing; I closed it myself this morning.

examples: She is {undoubtedly} the best player.
wrong: She is undoubtedly the best, but I really doubt it.

examples: The test was {relatively} easy.
wrong: The test was relatively easy, compared with nothing at all.

examples: Prices have risen {considerably}.
wrong: Prices rose considerably, by only one cent.

words.meaning: Close to an exact number, but not exactly.
examples: The trip takes {approximately} two hours.
wrong: It takes approximately two hours, exactly to the second.

examples: {Roughly} fifty people came.
wrong: Roughly fifty people came, exactly fifty and no more or less.

examples: It was {merely} a suggestion.
wrong: It was merely a huge, life-changing decision.

examples: The course is {primarily} for beginners.
wrong: The course is primarily for beginners, but almost no beginners take it.

examples: The plan was {largely} successful.
wrong: The plan was largely successful, although almost every part failed.

examples: {Initially}, I didn’t like the city.
wrong: Initially, at the very end, I liked it.

examples: He was arrested and {subsequently} released.
wrong: He was released and subsequently arrested before that.

words.meaning: In the end, after a long process.
examples: {Ultimately}, the decision is yours.
wrong: Ultimately, at the very start, we chose the blue one.

examples: The road was closed, {hence} the delay.
wrong: The road was open and clear, hence the long delay.

examples: We have a system {whereby} staff can work from home.
wrong: We have a system whereby, which is good.

examples: {Notwithstanding} the cost, we went ahead.
wrong: Notwithstanding the low cost, we went ahead because it was cheap.
